newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Fat finance sector may impede Asian growth-report.
newsitem.headline: Fat finance sector may impede Asian growth-report.

text.p: Protectionism in Asia's financial sector could impede the region's future economic growth unless major reforms to liberalize the industry are initiated, a report has warned.

Outside of Hong Kong and Singapore, "the local financial systems are increasingly inadequate in servicing the needs of these same countries' industrial and consumer sectors," said the Asian Intelligence report put out by the Hong Kong-based Political and Economic Risk Consultancy (PERC).

The report, a copy of which was made available on Sunday, said pressure was growing on the financial sector to reform but that there is resistance from "vested interest in the industry" and "certain parts of the government bureaucracy."
"In some countries, this (protectionism) has resulted in local banks growing fat and lazy on wide margins between deposits and loans," PERC said.
Noting that Singapore and Hong Kong "stand in stark contrast" to the other Asian countries, PERC ranked these two countries' banking systems as the best in the region, even ahead of Japan's.

In its survey of senior members of 30 of the largest banks in Europe and the U.S., PERC ranked Singapore number one, ahead of Hong Kong -- despite the colony's better banking system -- due primarily to uncertainty surrounding the handover of Hong Kong from Britain to China on July 1.

"It is not that Hong Kong's banking system is internally unstable, but the July 1 transition has clearly raised some doubts in foreign bankers' minds about how the financial sector could be affect," the report said.

PERC also noted the traumatic shake-outs seen in the U.S. and European banking sector, where massive layoffs and mergers have become common as banks push hard to embrace the latest technological innovations and stay competitive .

"By comparison, the banking systems in most Asian countries are standing still. There is no sense of urgency to restructure. This is clearly not because banks in Asia are so much better than those in the U.S. and Europe...(but) because they have been able to hide behind protective walls," PERC said.
PERC said the more industrialised countries of Asia -- Taiwan, Korea and Japan -- have the least-developed financial sectors.
Japan, it said, "is an example of a country with a first-rate industrial structure and a second-rate banking system. This mix has left the economy anemic."

The report concluded that there could be major opportunities for more competitive Western banks to make inroads in the Asian financial sector if they find a way to overcome the protectionist barriers.
This would benefit consumers and businesses in the region, it said.
